title: Arrays and Strings
summary: The two most common containers in interviews: boxes in a row, and text built from those boxes.
keyPoints: An array stores items in contiguous slots, so reading by index is O(1).
Inserting or deleting near the front shifts the remaining items, which costs O(n).
Python strings and JavaScript strings are immutable; each change creates a new string unless you collect pieces first.
Many array problems become simpler with a pass that counts, marks, or collects instead of repeatedly searching.

complexity.note: The slot address is computed directly.

complexity.operation: Insert or delete in the middle

complexity.note: Every item may need a check.
The bound depends on the sorting algorithm.

complexity.operation: Concatenate a string in a loop
complexity.note: Each concatenation may copy the whole string.

commonMistakes: Assuming string concatenation is free inside a loop; collect characters and join once.
Shifting the whole array for every removal instead of using a write index.
Forgetting that a string can contain punctuation, digits, spaces, or Unicode code points that are not single bytes.
interviewNotes: Say whether the input may be modified. If it may, an in-place solution can save O(n) memory.
Ask whether the string is ASCII or Unicode before indexing it by character; the answer affects the approach.
When a result is built piece by piece, mention the final join explicitly so the complexity is not accidentally quadratic.

checkYourself.question: Why is inserting at the front of an array O(n)?
checkYourself.answer: Every existing item must move one slot to the right to make room, so the work grows with the number of items.

checkYourself.question: Why is `result += ch` inside a loop risky for long strings?
checkYourself.answer: Each concatenation may copy the entire current result. Collecting pieces in a list and joining once avoids repeated copying.

checkYourself.question: How can you remove duplicates from a sorted array in place?
checkYourself.answer: Keep a write index for the next unique value. Scan with a read index and copy only new values forward.
